meta.title: The Bookbinder’s Letter
meta.subtitle: a story in three parts
meta.author: Josephine Estrada
meta.description: A bookbinder in Florence finds a letter hidden in the spine of a book a man brings in to be saved.

sections.title: Title Page
sections.plateAlt: A bookbinder's bench in Florence at dusk: a half-bound book under river stones, a brass lamp, and three red roses on the sill

sections.title: Dedication
sections.content:
For everyone who has
ever kept a letter.

sections.title: A Note on This Edition
sections.content:
*This little book is made to be held. It is set in a small, hand-sized format, on cream pages, with generous margins for thumbs and for notes in the margins. The titles are written in flowing script, because some stories should look the way they feel when they are read aloud — slowly, and by lamplight.*

*There is only one picture in this book, on the cover. Everything after it is left to the words, and to you.*

sections.title: The Shop on the Narrow Street
sections.subtitle: Part One
sections.content:
Elena’s shop was the smallest on the narrow street, and the quietest. It smelled of paper dust and warm glue, of leather and winter rain coming in through the door that never quite closed. On the bench by the window, a half-bound book waited under a weight of river stones, and on the sill a vase held three red roses that were already beginning, very politely, to fall apart.

She had inherited the shop from her father, and his father before him, and she had kept it exactly as it was: the same brass lamp, the same spools of linen thread, the same sign, painted by hand, that read Legatoria — bookbinding — in letters that had faded to the colour of tea. People came to her not when a book was new, but when it was loved. Loved books arrive in a particular state: soft at the corners, broken at the hinge, with a name written on the flyleaf in a hand that is no longer young.

On a Tuesday in late November, when the light over Florence had turned the colour of old gold, a man came in carrying such a book. It was a small volume of poems, its cloth cover stained dark by water at one corner, its pages rippled like a shoreline. He held it the way people hold something that has already survived one disaster and must not be asked to survive another.

“My mother read this to me,” he said, “when I was too small to read it myself. I dropped it in the river last spring. Not far in,” he added, quickly, as if the river might forgive him if the fault were small. “Only the edge. Can it be saved?”

Elena took the book and opened it the way she always did, slowly, listening for what the binding would tell her. “It can,” she said. “A book that has been read to a child is never really ruined. It only needs to be sewn again, and given a cover that will hold it for the next reader.” His name, he told her, was Matteo. He taught the cello to children who, he said, played mostly with great enthusiasm and very little regard for the neighbours.

***

She worked on the book that week in the long, lamp-lit evenings. She lifted the old cover away, cleaned the pages one by one, and dried them between sheets of blotting paper weighted with stones. It was while she was easing the last gathering apart that she found it: a letter, folded small, tucked into the hollow of the spine where no reader would ever have looked. It was not in his mother’s hand. The paper was older than the book, the ink a faded brown, the writing sloping and certain.

Elena did not read it. She set it on the bench, washed her hands, and looked at it for a long time, the way one looks at a door one has not been invited to open. A letter hidden in a binding is not quite a lost thing, and not quite a kept thing. It is a sentence left halfway between two lives. When Matteo came back on Friday, she put the letter on the counter between them, untouched.

“It was in the spine,” she said. “It is not mine to read, and it is not quite yours. But it was travelling with your book, so it belongs, at least, to this decision.” Matteo looked at the letter, and then at her, and smiled a little, as if he had been expecting something of the sort from a shop like this. “Then we will read only the first line,” he said. “Together. And if it asks us to stop, we will stop.”

sections.title: The Letter
sections.subtitle: Part Two
sections.content:
::: letter
If you are reading this, I stayed.
:::

That was the first line. Nothing more was needed to change the air in the shop. Elena read it aloud, softly, and Matteo did not speak for a moment. Then he laughed, quietly, the way people laugh when they have been caught out by kindness.

“I stayed,” he repeated. “I almost did not. Ten years ago I was offered a place in an orchestra in Vienna. I had the letter in my pocket for a week. I kept taking it out and putting it back, as if the pocket might decide for me. In the end my mother fell ill, and the decision was made by something larger than ambition. I stayed. I taught children to play the cello, badly and joyfully, and I never left Florence again. I have never regretted it in the way people mean when they say that word. I have only wondered, sometimes, what the other life sounded like.”

Elena understood that kind of wondering. She had stayed too. She had stayed with the shop, with the lamp and the stones and the sign in faded letters, while friends married and moved and wrote postcards from cities whose names sounded like music. Staying, she had learned, is not the same as standing still. A bookbinder stays in one room and travels, every day, through other people’s lives.

They read the rest of the letter together, after all — not because they had a right to it, but because the letter itself seemed to be asking to be read, the way a song asks to be sung once before it is put away. It was written by a woman to a man she had loved and not married, telling him, without anger, that she had chosen a different road, and that she wished him well on his. There was no bitterness in it. Only the clear, tired honesty of someone who had made a choice and then made a life around it, the way a binder makes a cover around a text: carefully, and to last.

When they had finished, Elena folded the letter again, exactly along its old creases, and Matteo said, “We should put it back. Not hidden — kept. A book can carry a letter the way a house can carry a photograph. It does not have to explain it.” So Elena made a small pocket of cream linen and sewed it into the new binding, where the letter could live, safe and findable, for whoever opened the book next.

***

After that, Matteo came back every week, although the book was nearly done. He brought coffee in paper cups and stories about his pupils, one of whom had named her cello Beatrice and apologised to it whenever she played a wrong note. Elena showed him how to sew a gathering, and he showed her, very patiently, how to hold a bow without strangling it. The shop, which had been quiet for years, began to sound like a place where two people were learning, at the same unhurried pace, how to stay in the same room.

One evening, when the rain had stopped and the street was shining, they walked together to the river. The Arno was dark and gold by turns, and the city was doing what Florence does best at dusk: pretending, for an hour, that time is a generous thing. Matteo stopped on the bridge and said, “I used to think a life was something you chose once, and then lived with. Now I think it is something you choose again, in small ways, every day. Like returning a book to the shelf. Like coming back to a shop.” Elena did not answer at once. She was listening to the water, and to something else, quieter, that had begun to sound a great deal like hope.

sections.title: The Binding
sections.subtitle: Part Three
sections.content:
The binding was finished on the first clear morning of December. Elena chose a deep red cloth, the colour of the roses on her sill, and lined it with cream paper the colour of winter light. She sewed the gatherings with linen thread, rounded the spine, and set the title in small gold letters that caught the lamp and gave it back, gently. The book that had gone into the river came out of her hands looking, not new — Elena never made a loved book look new — but whole. Held. Ready for the next reader, whoever that might be.

Before she closed the cover for the last time, she did one more thing. She took a sheet of her own cream paper, and in her own sloping hand she wrote a letter. It was not long. It did not ask for anything grand. It said, simply, what she had learned from a letter she had not been meant to read: that staying is also a kind of courage, and that a shop, a street, a city, and a person can all be kept, lovingly, by returning to them.

::: letter
Come back on Thursday, if you like. The coffee will be hot, and the lamp will be on.
:::

She slipped her letter into the linen pocket beside the older one, and closed the book. When Matteo came to collect it, he held it for a long time without opening it, the way he had held it when he first brought it in. “It feels,” he said, “like something that has been listened to.” Elena smiled. “That is what binding is,” she said. “Listening, with thread.”

He found her letter that evening, at home, by lamplight. He read it twice, folded it back along its crease, and put it in his coat pocket, where it stayed, warm and certain, all the way back across the city the next morning. Elena was at her bench when the bell over the door rang. She did not look up at once. She was sewing, and sewing requires attention. But when she did look up, Matteo was standing there with two paper cups of coffee, and with the particular expression of a man who has read a letter and decided, at last, what to do about it.

“Thursday,” he said. “And Friday. And, if the shop will have me, most days after that.” Elena put down her needle. Outside, the light over Florence was turning gold again, and the roses on the sill, against all expectation, were holding on for one more day. She took the coffee, and she took his hand, and she said the thing she had been practising, quietly, for a week: “Stay.”

::: center
*Some books are not finished*

*when they are bound.*

*Some are only beginning.*
:::

sections.title: Colophon
sections.content:
The Bookbinder’s Letter is an original story, written for this little edition. It is not a retelling of any other book, and its people, its shop, and its letters are invented.

Designed as a small, hand-sized book — A5, with cream pages and generous margins — to be printed, folded, kept on a shelf, and lent to someone who will love it a little more with every reading.

::: center
*The End*
:::
